title: The centurion glorifies God (Luke 23:44–49)
hook: Indeed this was a just man, and the crowds go home beating their breasts

segments.voice: Yesterday, Father: the first word from the cross, Father, forgive them. Your line was they know not.

At every Mass, near the start, Catholics say the Confiteor, the I confess. At the words through my fault, the missal has the people strike their breast: a small, old gesture, a closed hand to the chest. Where does it come from? One place it shows up is today's reading. About the sixth hour, around noon, on the day of the crucifixion, darkness comes over the whole earth until the ninth hour. The veil of the temple is torn down the middle. Jesus cries out with a loud voice, and dies. Then Luke turns the camera away from the cross, to the people standing in front of it.
screen: `A HAND TO THE CHEST AT MASS.` → `DARKNESS AT THE SIXTH HOUR.` → `THE CAMERA TURNS TO THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: Luke's Jesus dies with a psalm on his lips: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." It's from Psalm thirty, thirty-one in other Bibles, a prayer of trust the Church prays at Compline, its prayer before sleep. Then Luke shows three reactions. First, the centurion, the Roman officer in charge, who watched it all up close: "Now the centurion, seeing what was done, glorified God, saying: Indeed this was a just man." Matthew and Mark have him say Son of God. Luke has a just man, innocent, righteous, and frames it as praise: the first reaction Luke reports after the death is a Roman officer glorifying God. Second, the crowds. They came to see a spectacle, and they go home striking their breasts. No speech, just a gesture of grief and something like guilt. Third, his friends. All his acquaintances, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, stood afar off, watching. They can't do anything. They stay. Some see clearly and say so. Some feel it in the chest and go home changed. Some refuse to look away. Catholic devotion names that last kind from the old hymn Stabat Mater, the mother standing. Luke doesn't name Mary here; John does. But the women who watch him die are the women who will go to the tomb.
screen: `INTO THY HANDS.` · `A SOLDIER SAYS: A JUST MAN.` · `THE CROWD STRIKES THEIR BREASTS.` · `THE WOMEN STAND AFAR OFF.`

segments.voice: If there's a crucifix near you, look at it; if not, picture one, or simply that hill in the afternoon dark. Don't try to feel anything in particular; just stay, the way the women stayed, afar off and watching, and come back to the picture when your mind wanders. If you pray, say his last line from the psalm, into thy hands; if you don't, just keep your attention there.
Dikaios. The Greek word for just, righteous, innocent: what the centurion called Jesus at the cross when he glorified God. Today's word.
Your line: a just man. A Roman soldier's words, said as praise. That's day four hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's account of the death in the Palm Sunday Passion in the year of Luke, and pray "into thy hands" from Psalm 31 each night at Compline; at Mass they strike the breast during the Confiteor.

chat.says: What did the Roman soldier at the cross actually say when Jesus died?
options: In Luke he glorified God and said, indeed this was a just man: innocent, righteous.
In Luke he asked Pilate for the body so he could bury Jesus himself.
In Luke he said nothing, and went home striking his breast with the crowd.
chat.meaning: Luke says the centurion, seeing what was done, glorified God: indeed this was a just man. Dikaios: just, righteous, innocent.

notes: The breast-striking at the Confiteor is linked to Luke 23:48 as 'one place it shows up', not as its origin (the publican, Luke 18:13, is also cited). Confirm.
Compline: Psalm 31's 'into thy hands' is the responsory at Night Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours. Confirm.
Psalm numbering: Psalm 30 in the Douay/Vulgate, 31 in Hebrew-numbered Bibles. Confirm the voice's phrasing.
Confirm exact Douay wording of Luke 23:46–47.
Stabat Mater mentioned only as a name for the devotion of standing at the cross; confirm.
